newsitem.title: UK: Adams urges IRA to call new ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Adams urges IRA to call new ceasefire.

text.p: The head of the IRA's political wing urged the republican guerrillas on Friday to call a new truce in their 28-year war against British rule in Northern Ireland.
Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, said he would not have asked the IRA to call a new ceasefire if he had not been confident of a positive response.

A Sinn Fein statement said Adams and its chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, had "provided a detailed report and assessment to the IRA (Irish Republican Army) and has urged the IRA leadership to restore its cessation of August 1994".
The IRA ended its 17- month ceasefire in February 1996 by setting off a powerful bomb in London's docklands.

Amid rising hopes that the Irish Republican Army would again call off hostilities and pave the way for Sinn Fein to enter all-party talks, Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern said he warmly welcomed the move.
"I trust and hope that their response will be positive as this would be very good news for all the people of Ireland," Ahern said.

"If an IRA ceasefire now follows, I look forward to the opening of inclusive and substantive all-party talks in September. We must all unite to consolidate peace and to ensure that the gun in Irish politics is silenced for the last time."
Some key politicians from the province's pro-British Protestant minority voiced scepticism about the prospect of a fresh truce by the republican guerrillas.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the hardline pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said he was suspicious that any IRA ceasefire would be a ploy simply to get Sinn Fein to the talks table.
"The IRA are calling another tactical cessation of violence. People were fooled before and surely they are not going to allow themselves to be fooled and suckered once more by the IRA.

"It (a ceasefire) is there in order to extract concessions from the British government and unfortunately we have got a very weak government and one that is capable of making concessions to them," he told BBC television.

In a statement that took politicians in Britain and Ireland by surprise, Adams signalled he was satisfied that the London and Dublin governments were committed to holding unconditional "inclusive peace talks".
"The process of obtaining detail and clarity on these issues has been painstaking but essential," Adams said.
On his request that the guerrillas should restore the truce that collapsed last year , Adams said: "The IRA leadership assured us that they would respond without delay to our request."
Republican sources were unable to say precisely how long the commanders of the outlawed underground force would take to respond to the Sinn Fein leaders' urging.

"I have made it clear over the 18 months since the collapse of the peace process that I would only approach the IRA to restore their cessation if I was confident that their reponse would be positive," Adams declared
"If the political will exists there is the potential to resolve the conflict on the basis of an agreed and democratic peace settlement among all the Irish people," Adams said.
"There is an onus on the two governments, and in particular on the British government, to demonstrate the political will necessary."

Ken Maginnis, a spokesman for the chief pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) which insists that the IRA must surrender guns before Sinn Fein is allowed into full negotiations, said his group would not take anything the IRA says at face value.

"We will be looking for a complete, permanent and universal ending of violence, plus very quick disarmament and disbandment of the terrorist organisations that have plagued us for 25 years," Maginnis told BBC raido.

However, Denis Haughey, a senior official of the main pro-Irish Catholic SDLP nationalist applauded Adams's call, describing it as a very hopeful and significant development. "I think we all trust and pray that the IRA will respond quickly and positively to it."
Adams indicated he had received assurances that demands for a surrender of IRA weaponry would not be allowed to block negotiations.
Britain has consistently said that the IRA must abandon violence for Sinn Fein to be given a seat in all-party talks.
It says that Sinn Fein could enter talks six weeks after an unequivocal end to violence by the guerrillas.

Protestant pro-British "loyalist" guerrillas, the IRA's foes on the other side of Northern Ireland's political and sectarian divide, insist a ceasefire they declared in October 1994 remains intact, despite several killings they have been accused of carrying out.
